implementation_notes: The original Vapor realization returns an EventLoopFuture: the middleware calls next.respond(to: request) and maps or flatMaps the future to post-process the response, and it short-circuits by returning a failed future such as request.eventLoop.future(error: Abort(.unauthorized)). It works on any supported Swift version without concurrency features, and it composes cleanly with other future-based code, at the cost of leaving callback chains inside the filter.
pitfalls: A failed future ends the chain silently from the caller's perspective: unrelated errors surface as bare 500s unless mapped to an Abort.
Blocking operations inside a future callback run on an event loop thread and starve the whole server; hop to a thread pool instead of sleeping there.
Forgetting to return the transformed future loses the post-processing step entirely - the compiler will not warn.

variants.name: Vapor AsyncMiddleware (Swift concurrency)
variants.implementation_notes: With Swift 5.5 and later the same chain can be written with async/await: AsyncMiddleware declares respond(to:chainingTo:) async throws -> Response, delegation is try await next.respond(to: request), and a guard that fails simply throws Abort(.unauthorized) to short-circuit. The pre- and post-processing become straight-line code with real error propagation, which is why this is the preferred form for new code on modern toolchains.
pitfalls: Mixing the two protocols on one type is not supported: pick Middleware or AsyncMiddleware for a given filter and register it consistently.
A middleware that throws after awaiting the response still runs during response transmission, so errors there surface as truncated responses.
Structured cancellation must be propagated by awaiting the responder chain; spawning a detached task inside a filter breaks request-scoped cleanup.
